name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MCQ_Q01 - Physical quantities and their SI units

questiontext.text:
Match the physical quantities in List-I with their corresponding SI units in List-II:

List-IList-II
(A) Electrostatic potential(I) \(\text{C}\cdot\text{m}^{-2}\)
(B) Capacitance(II) \(\text{J}\cdot\text{m}^{-3}\)
(C) Electric polarisation(III) \(\text{V}\)
(D) Electrostatic energy density(IV) \(\text{F}\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Electrostatic potential, capacitance, polarisation, and electrostatic energy density are standard physical quantities defined in electrostatics.

Step 2: Analysis of First Pair
Electrostatic potential is the work done per unit test charge, \(V = \frac{W}{q}\), with SI unit of volt (\(\text{V}\), equivalent to \(\text{J}\cdot\text{C}^{-1}\)).

Step 3: Analysis of Second Pair
Capacitance is the ratio of stored charge to potential difference, \(C = \frac{Q}{V}\), with SI unit of farad (\(\text{F}\), equivalent to \(\text{C}\cdot\text{V}^{-1}\)).

Step 4: Analysis of Third Pair
Electric polarisation represents the dipole moment per unit volume, \(\mathbf{P} = \frac{\mathbf{p}}{\Delta v}\), having the SI unit of coulomb per square metre (\(\text{C}\cdot\text{m}^{-2}\)).

Step 5: Analysis of Fourth Pair
Electrostatic energy density is the energy stored per unit volume of the electric field, \(u = \frac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 E^2\), which has the SI unit of joule per cubic metre (\(\text{J}\cdot\text{m}^{-3}\)).

Step 6: Final Conclusion
Matching each physical quantity with its unit yields: Electrostatic potential corresponds to \(\text{V}\); Capacitance corresponds to \(\text{F}\); Electric polarisation corresponds to \(\text{C}\cdot\text{m}^{-2}\); Electrostatic energy density corresponds to \(\text{J}\cdot\text{m}^{-3}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MCQ_Q02 - Electrostatic field and potential distance dependence

questiontext.text:
Match each electrostatic configuration in List-I with its characteristic spatial dependence in List-II:

List-IList-II
(A) Electric potential due to an isolated point charge(I) Zero everywhere
(B) Electric field magnitude due to an isolated point charge(II) Varies inversely as \(r\)
(C) Electric potential on the equatorial plane of an electric dipole(III) Varies inversely as \(r^2\)
(D) Electric field magnitude of a short dipole at large axial distance(IV) Varies inversely as \(r^3\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The distance dependence of electric fields and potentials depends on the multipole order of the source charge distribution.

Step 2: Analysis of First Pair
For an isolated monopole point charge \(q\), the electric potential is \(V(r) = \frac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r}\), which varies inversely with distance as \(1/r\).

Step 3: Analysis of Second Pair
The electric field of an isolated point charge is governed by Coulomb's law, \(E(r) = \frac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r^2}\), exhibiting an inverse-square dependence as \(1/r^2\).

Step 4: Analysis of Third Pair
For an electric dipole, the potential at any point is \(V(r, \theta) = \frac{p\cos\theta}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r^2}\). On the equatorial plane, \(\theta = 90^\circ\) and \(\cos 90^\circ = 0\), meaning the potential is identically zero everywhere on this plane.

Step 5: Analysis of Fourth Pair
Along the axial line of a short electric dipole, the electric field at large distance (\(r \gg a\)) is \(E = \frac{2p}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r^3}\), falling off inversely as the cube of distance, \(1/r^3\).

Step 6: Final Conclusion
Matching each configuration with its spatial variation yields: Electric potential of a point charge corresponds to varying inversely as \(r\); Electric field of a point charge corresponds to varying inversely as \(r^2\); Potential on dipole equatorial plane corresponds to zero everywhere; Electric field of a short dipole on axis corresponds to varying inversely as \(r^3\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MCQ_Q03 - Capacitor parameters under dielectric insertion

questiontext.text:
A parallel plate capacitor with initial parameters \(C_0\), \(Q_0\), \(V_0\), and \(U_0\) is filled with a dielectric slab of constant \(K > 1\). Match the condition in List-I with the resulting parameter in List-II:

List-IList-II
(A) Capacitance of the capacitor with the dielectric slab present(I) Decreases to \(V_0 / K\)
(B) Potential difference across the plates when dielectric is inserted with battery disconnected(II) Increases to \(K C_0\)
(C) Charge on the plates when dielectric is inserted with battery remaining connected(III) Decreases to \(U_0 / K\)
(D) Electrostatic energy stored when dielectric is inserted with battery disconnected(IV) Increases to \(K Q_0\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor completely filled with a dielectric of constant \(K\) becomes \(C = K C_0\), irrespective of external circuit connections.

Step 2: Analysis of First Pair
The capacitance increases from \(C_0\) to \(K C_0\) due to dielectric polarization neutralizing a fraction of the surface charge field.

Step 3: Analysis of Second Pair
When the charging battery is disconnected prior to inserting the slab, the plate charge remains isolated and conserved at \(Q = Q_0\). Consequently, the potential difference becomes \(V = \frac{Q_0}{C} = \frac{Q_0}{K C_0} = \frac{V_0}{K}\), decreasing by a factor of \(K\).

Step 4: Analysis of Third Pair
When the battery remains connected, the potential difference is actively fixed at \(V = V_0\). The new stored charge is \(Q = C V_0 = (K C_0) V_0 = K Q_0\), increasing by a factor of \(K\).

Step 5: Analysis of Fourth Pair
With the battery disconnected, the stored electrostatic energy is \(U = \frac{Q_0^2}{2C} = \frac{Q_0^2}{2 K C_0} = \frac{U_0}{K}\), decreasing by a factor of \(K\) as electrostatic work is done by the field on the slab.

Step 6: Final Conclusion
Matching each scenario with its resulting value yields: Capacitance with dielectric corresponds to increasing to \(K C_0\); Potential difference with battery disconnected corresponds to decreasing to \(V_0 / K\); Charge with battery connected corresponds to increasing to \(K Q_0\); Stored energy with battery disconnected corresponds to decreasing to \(U_0 / K\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MCQ_Q04 - Electrostatic states of conductors and dipoles

questiontext.text:
Match each electrostatic system in List-I with its physical state or property in List-II:

List-IList-II
(A) Charge-free cavity inside an arbitrarily shaped conductor(I) Electric field is \(\frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}\hat{\mathbf{n}}\) normal to the surface
(B) Outer surface of a charged conductor with local surface charge density \(\sigma\)(II) Torque is zero and potential energy is at its minimum of \(-pE\)
(C) Electric dipole aligned parallel to a uniform electric field(III) Electric field is strictly zero regardless of external fields
(D) Electric dipole aligned perpendicular to a uniform electric field(IV) Torque is maximum at \(pE\) and potential energy is zero

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Electrostatic equilibrium in conductors enforces specific boundary conditions, and the potential energy of a dipole in an external field is given by \(U = -\mathbf{p}\cdot\mathbf{E} = -pE\cos\theta\) with torque \(\boldsymbol{\tau} = \mathbf{p} \times \mathbf{E}\).

Step 2: Analysis of First Pair
By the principle of electrostatic shielding, any empty cavity within a conductor remains completely shielded from external electrical fields, ensuring that the electric field inside the cavity is strictly zero.

Step 3: Analysis of Second Pair
By Gauss's law applied across the conducting boundary, the electrostatic field just outside a charged conductor is \(E = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}\), oriented strictly perpendicular to the conducting surface.

Step 4: Analysis of Third Pair
When a dipole is aligned parallel to the field (\(\theta = 0^\circ\)), \(\sin 0^\circ = 0\) so the torque is zero, and \(\cos 0^\circ = 1\) so the potential energy reaches its global minimum, \(U_{\min} = -pE\) (stable equilibrium).

Step 5: Analysis of Fourth Pair
When a dipole is oriented perpendicular to the field (\(\theta = 90^\circ\)), the torque reaches its maximum value of \(\tau = pE\sin 90^\circ = pE\), while the potential energy is \(U = -pE\cos 90^\circ = 0\).

Step 6: Final Conclusion
Matching each system with its state yields: Charge-free cavity corresponds to electric field strictly zero; Outer surface of conductor corresponds to field of \(\frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}\hat{\mathbf{n}}\); Dipole parallel to field corresponds to zero torque and minimum energy \(-pE\); Dipole perpendicular to field corresponds to maximum torque \(pE\) and zero energy.
